claim: A 12-page document describing an alleged Pentagon program called "Immaculate Constellation" is in the Congressional Record. Journalist Michael Shellenberger delivered it to Congress and it was entered without objection at the joint hearing "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth" on November 13, 2024, before two subcommittees of the House Oversight and Accountability Committee (Serial No. 118-135); the hearing's index of documents lists it as "Report, Pentagon, 'Immaculate Constellation'; submitted by Rep. Mace." The document itself is filed as a supporting exhibit and can be read. Its author is anonymous in the public version and identifies as a Department of Defense employee who obtained the material "while pursuing their lawful duties," submitting it through the UAP whistleblower channels created by the FY23 National Defense Authorization Act and the FY23 Intelligence Authorization Act; it states that "this public version of the author's report was reviewed and approved for public release by the Department of State, Bureau of Global Public Affairs." It alleges that "elements of the U.S. Executive Branch have conspired to prevent the U.S. Legislative Branch from exercising its lawful powers of governance" over UAP, and describes Immaculate Constellation as an unacknowledged special access program established after Luis Elizondo's 2017 disclosure of AATIP, acting as "a central or 'parent' USAP that consolidates observations of UAP and ARV activities detected by tasked and untasked collection platforms." It organizes its material into seven categories — the program itself, imagery intelligence, human intelligence drawn from a review of "over 400 defense HUMINT reports," signals intelligence, DoD bureaucratic records, restricted historical records, and sensitive sources. It alleges that DoD briefings to Congress show "a pattern of trivialization, obfuscation, and outright denial of UAP data," including denying Immaculate Constellation's existence to members and staff. Two things limit what the document can carry on its own: its seventh evidence category is given in full as "From mouth to ear," and it closes not with findings but with an exhortation — "Be not afraid" — under a Latin motto. Asked whether he had been read into the program, witness Luis Elizondo said: "Ma'am, I would not be authorized to confirm nor deny the existence of any ongoing or past program, especially as it relates to a special access program, either by name or trigraph." A Department of Defense spokesperson said it had no records of such a program. No government source has confirmed it.

notes: Backstage. Upgraded from citing the hearing to citing the document: pulled the exhibit itself (SD003) off the committee repository, rasterized and OCR'd it — the filing is a 1-bit CCITT scan with no text layer, so pdftotext returns nothing and OCR is required. The distinction the card holds: a document being entered into the Congressional Record is a documented fact about the document and says nothing about whether its contents are true. Both halves stated. The Department of State prepublication-review line is the document's own assertion and is quoted as such — not independently confirmed, and worth chasing, because if true it is the strongest institutional fact in the whole cluster. Deliberately included the two lines that undercut it ('From mouth to ear'; 'Be not afraid') rather than only its strongest passages — a card that quoted only the alarming parts would be doing the same selective work the reels do. Section 4's allegation about DoD denials is set against 2024-aaro-historical-record-001 rather than being used to dismiss it. OCR is tesseract --psm 6 on a 300dpi render; quotes were eyeballed against the page images before use. Group A on the document and its filing; every claim inside it is Group B.
